speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is to enable
inspectors of the court to approve payment of legal fees in excess of 5 per cent of the gross proceeds of the estate. In some cases assets have been lost because there was no provision to pay the necessary legal charges to recover them.

I would suggest to the minister that he strike out the words "in writing of the inspectors and" so that the amendment will read, "except with the approval of the court." My reason for the suggestion is that the trustee deciding to do certain work must first consult his inspectors under the provisions of the act. When he receives their authority he instructs the solicitor to go ahead. There are many cases where the value of the work is largely in excess of 5 per cent of the gross proceeds of the estate, and that is particularly true where the assignor holds large properties in trust for other persons. In fact a large portion of the assets may consist of these trust assets; the actual assets of the estate may be very small. In cases where the inspectors instruct the solicitor to go ahead and do the work, obviously the solicitor should be paid reasonable fees for doing that work. In practically all cases the court fixes the fee payable to solicitors or counsel. A tariff of fees is laid down and the court first directs taxation of the bill of the solicitor. I cannot see why it should be necessary to secure the approval of the inspectors in writing of such bill, because they do not understand what are proper fees to be paid the solicitors. The court, on the other hand, is dealing with that question every day, and I think it will be quite sufficient to leave it entirely to the court to say whether or not it is reasonable that a solicitor in a certain case should be paid more than the five per cent. If it i3 decided that he shall be paid more than five per cent, then it is fair to leave it to the registrar to decide by means of taxation what actual amount the solicitor should be allowed.
Does my hon. friend not think it would be better for the registrar to tax the costs in the first instance, and then if the parties are not agreeable, to have the judge decide the matter?

I am only suggesting what I think is the custom not only throughout Canada but in Great Britain as well. The court in all such matters directs the solicitor's account to be taxed by the registrar and then the registrar taxes it.

With all due deference to my hon. friend, I may say that the practice in our province is that the solicitor's bill is taxed by the taxing master. Certain fees are prescribed; there is a maximum and a minimum, and the maximum can only be exceeded when the court or a judge so rules. If a solicitor is not satisfied, he may appeal to a judge for a rehearing and retaxation.

That is not the point at all. This is a case where it must be decided in the first instance whether or not a solicitor shall be at liberty to present a bill. The court decides that; it is decided every day in winding-up proceedings. When the court decides that the solicitor is entitled to present a bill, then it goes to the taxing master, who taxes it. If the solicitor is not satisfied with his bill he has the right to appeal to the judge as my hon. friend has suggested.

I am not familiar with the system of taxation in the various provinces, but does my hon. friend mean to say that a solicitor is entitled to have costs taxed where the act does not entitle him to costs?
No; my hon. friend has not followed me at all. He has not got the point.

I suggest that where the money procurable from the insolvent's estate is not sufficient to pay the solicitor's fees, the solicitor himself shall become one of the creditors and go on a pro rata basis the same as the rest.

On section 1-Revocation of fiat obtained by fraud.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendment is to authorize the Governor in Council to revoke any fiat which he might have granted on a petition of right whenever he discovers that the granting of such fiat was induced by misrepresentation, concealment or non-disclosure on the part of the petitioner of any material fact which in the minister's opinion should have been truly stated or disclosed for the minister's information in the consideration of the petition. Passing an order in council revoking such fiat and depositing that order in council with the clerk of the court, puts an end to the case. Here is how subsection 2 reads:
A copy of any order in council revoking or withdrawing the Governor General's fiat upon any petition of right as aforesaid, certified by the clerk of the Privy Council, may be filed in the Exchequer Court, and thereupon the petition shall abate, and all further proceedings in the action shall be and be deemed to have been, by the revocation or withdrawal of the fiat, perpetually stayed.
This bill looks to be a perfectly proper bill, but I suppose it was brought in for the purpose of correcting the mistake of the government in granting the fiat in the famous Hoppe lease case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We do not admit tve ever committed an error. There is not legislation to cover any special case. We only thought it was advisable to make our position perfectly clear, that whenever a fiat had been granted and we discovered that we were misinformed or deceived we would have the right to revoke such fiat.
I am quite sure, Mr. Chairman, that the coincidence is just simply something that is remarkable.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It just synchronizes.

The synchronization is really complete. It is perfectly wonderful that just after a committee of the Senate dealing with the Hoppe case recommends such legislation this legislation is brought down and there is no connection between the two at all. Well, Mr. Chairman,
Petition of Right Act

apparently we have not got out of the age of miracles yet.
Does the hon. member believe in miracles?
I never did before but I am asked to believe in them tonight.
I am glad to see you are waking up.

My hon. friend is perfectly correct, Mr. Chairman. It is a great thing to brighten up, and it is a great thing to be able to listen to the declarations now made by the minister without a smile of incredulity. I ask my hon. friends though seriously whether it is not a fact that the Hoppe leases were referred to a committee of the Senate, and that as a result of its inquiries such a state of affairs was ascertained that the department presided over so ably by my hon. friend-I do not say he did it- recommended that the fiat should be withdrawn, stated that if the facts had been known the fiat would never 'have been given, and that this bill is necessary for the purpose of carrying that report into egect. Am I not right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

An investigation took place in the Senate into the Hoppe leases. I said at the outset in explaining the bill and in answer to my hon. friend that this was not legislation specially brought down for the Isenberg estate. This bill was introduced in the Senate so as to make our position perfectly clear, that there should be no doubt as to our right to revoke such fiats whether it be in the Isenberg case, or any other case that might be now pending or arising in the future. There is no mystery in the whole thing. If my hon. friend is satisfied that this is good legislation, he should approve of it and let it pass.

I quite understand that my learned friend is in one sense perfectly right. He is perfectly right when he says that this is not a special private act which is passed for the purpose of undoing (Sil Henry Drayton.]
the mistake of granting the fiat in the Hoppe case. That is perfectly true. Before the section carries I wish to explain why I asked one or two questions. Probably I am a little hoarse and my hon. friend opposite did not quite understand me. I asked those questions with a view to securing information. I have a little

Petition oj Right Act
but not great familiarity with the question of petitions of right. Every subject has a right to petition the sovereign and the Crown has the right to issue a fiat, which fiat issues in order that right may be done. But supposing any person applies for a petition of right and the Crown, as represented by the cabinet ministers, refuses to grant that right; to whom should people appeal in order to have it declared whether they have been rightly or wrongly denied that right? Now, irrespective of what party may be in power persons will apply for a petition of right. I have in mind a case where a petition of right was refused and by the party which I support. I believe we have a Supreme Court of Judicature in this country to which we refer all cases, whether constitutional or otherwise, in the form of a stated case, and that court should have the right to say finally whether or not a petition of right or a fiat should issue. If you do not do that people will never get justice in this country because politics will enter in and no minister will admit that he ever did wrong in his own department. That was my only reason in rising to ask questions of lawyers who have been longer at the bar, than I have touching this matter. I am sorry that I am a little hoarse to-night or I would have talked
11 p.m. at much greater length in protest against any cabinet, or any government having the power to say finally whether people should be denied the right to appeal to the courts of the land in order to have their cases tried on their merits. Now, as the case stands to-day a person may petition to the Minister of Justice for the issue of a fiat. Naturally the minister, in connection with whose department the petition is entered, is very apt to say, "We have done no wrong," and to go to the law officers of the Crown and argue his own case. I submit that should not be final. I believe it would be good legislation in this country, where a petition of right is denied by the government, to give the Supreme Court of Canada the right to say whether a fiat or petition of right should issue. That may be considered radical from a lawyer; but I consider that is the proper way to deal with the matter, because no man should be denied justice or deprived of an opportunity of contesting his rights in the courts of the land.

I should like to ask the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) a couple of questions, the first question for a matter of information. Supposing the Minister of Justice has been imposed upon, and a fiat has been granted by reason of some misrepresen-
tation or some fraudulent non-disclosure; would the minister not be entitled to cancel the fiat without any legislation whatever?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is possible, but we want to make it perfectly clear.
The second question that I want to ask the minister is whether or not he proposes, when this legislation is passed, to apply it to the Hoppe case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As to that we will consult our lawyers, and if it is applicable, we will apply it to that case.

I should like to have an answer as to whether there is any possibility of having my suggestion followed out. If there is argument in favour of a fiat or petition of right, could the matter not be carried to the Supreme Court 'of Canada to determine whether or not a fiat should issue in the event of the government deciding that it should not issue?

The hon. member
addressed the question to me in the first instance, and I say that there is no appeal. I may say to him that he has found a Minister of Justice big enough to say when he is wrong. He did give the fiat last year, and he is now saying that it ought not to have issued.
I am satisfied with the Minister of Justice, and he is a big man too.
